segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: We are glad that you could come this afternoon. The reason that they are recording Cherokee speakers is so they can use it here at this school to listen to the way Cherokee sounds when we are speaking it. And also, you speaking Cherokee will be preserved. Maybe your children or your family might want to listen. As we begin, what is your name in English?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: In English? Billy Teehee.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Wil(i).

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Just there at Salem. They didn’t take me to the doctor when I was born. I was just born at someone’s house a long time ago.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about your parents? What were their names?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: My dad’s name was (Tsali), and (Wonidi) was my mother. They raised me, but they were not my real parents. When I was little, someone gave me away. My mom’s name was (Svnugs). I guess she was not able to raise me. And (Tsali) and (Wonidi) took me in. I grew up there.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Are they related to you?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: (Tsali) is my grandfather.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: So, your grandpa and your grandma raised you?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yes, there were nine of us. I think of them as if they were my dad and mom. When they raised me, they did good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Really, even nowadays, there are a lot that are raising their grandkids, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, my grandchildren are living at my house now. I am raising them now, three of them. And when we lived at Salem, the nine of them, I don’t know if you want me to, but I can name them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: The oldest one they call him Raymond and the second born John. Am is my sister and another, her name is Ann. Udvyi, Svduli, Lee, and Gvwesdi. I was first. My name’s Will, and Gvwesdi was born last. There were nine of us that grew up in Salem.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When you said Lee, was it him that was married to that woman who used to be a Steeley?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, her name is Alene.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s it, I knew him.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: That is my brother.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s him.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: He was born before me. We are all about two years apart, all of us.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How many of you are still living?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: There are just three of us living. Me, Svduli, and the one named Gvwesdi, the last-born girl.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That one you are saying, Svduli, what is his name in English?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Amos Teehee. Paulie is his wife’s name. You have probably heard of their daughter, they call her Kim. Kim Teehee, they call her. She works there.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I have heard of her.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: She is a lawyer. Nowadays, she is a lawyer. That is my niece, you could say.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Your niece, is that it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, that is my family.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When you grew up in Salem, what was it like at that time? What could you do?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Well, it was woods - they call it Fog Hollow. Before Salem, we were practically the only ones living there. You could almost go all the way across. We were living on land that was given to us by the natives. We grew up just working around there. When I started school, I only spoke Cherokee. I didn’t speak English when I started.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Where did you start going to school?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: They call it Bell uyvlvni. Do they call it uyvlvni there? I went there for eight years, and then I came to Stilwell. It was there I learned to speak English. We all spoke Cherokee growing up. All of my family, they all speak Cherokee. Some can read the paper.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about you? Can you read?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, I can read pretty good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s good.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I can read almost anything.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What you are saying about Bell, I went to Greasy, and when I started, there were lots of us Cherokees. Most of us were, and the workers were Cherokee. At school, we spoke in Cherokee. I don’t ever remember having a rough time speaking English.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I didn’t either.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I guess I used a little bit of both... you could say.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: You can learn faster when you are just a child. You can learn faster to speak English or Cherokee. I learned to speak English there quickly. All of us children only spoke Cherokee when we started. In the mornings, a bus went by. We walked for about a mile to the road and caught the bus to the school, and it was also the same to Salem where we went to church. I don’t know if you know where that’s at.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yeah, I know where it is.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We walked there on Sunday mornings. And at noon, we would be walking back. It was about two miles. In the evening, we would do the same thing, and Wednesday, too. We all got around by walking. We didn’t have any cars.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The people really had energy back then, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: But we didn’t care. We were used to it. That’s just the way we lived back then.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you remember who the pastor was then at Salem?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: They called him Enoch Acorn. Enoch was his name. They preached in all Cherokee back then. There wasn’t any English preaching yet back then. They preached in all Cherokee. There was one named Chulio who lived on the mountain, also. He started when Enoch quit, or he passed away, and it was all in Cherokee, and his wife was the secretary. She would write everything for them in Cherokee. They didn’t use nothing in English. Everything was in Cherokee - the singing, everything. It didn’t change until sometime later. But that is what happens, because these children growing up now only speak English nowadays. That’s the reason that they started to preach only in English. But still in Cherokee, the teaching was still in Cherokee, but when they preached, they used lots of English. The reason was, some were there who did not understand Cherokee. That’s what happened. Nowadays, they just use English, but there are still a lot of Cherokee speakers.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Lawrence Eagle pastored there at Salem for a long time, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, we grew up with him at the same time. Lawrence was catching chickens. I did the same thing for a long time, too, until I started something different, but I also did that growing up. I knew all of them boys that live toward Salem and Greasy. We used to run around together. I knew a lot of them. Almost all of the older people who live at Greasy, Salem, and Bell - everywhere, I know them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Who were you helping when you used to catch chickens?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Myself. I had my own crew.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Who was it with, was it Peterson?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: When I started, I was helping Digi Watie. Then Lawrence started after that. Then, when I grew up a little bit, I started my own. But it was Georges in Springdale where I started.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It was Delmar Watie, the one you said was Digi?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, they called Delmar Digi and they called his brother Stewi.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yeah, Sundown.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, Sundown.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I know him, I grew up at Greasy. I, too, led chicken catchers. It was Peterson at first, then Simmons bought it. That is where I got to know all of the boys that live that way. The late Stoney?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, I knew him.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That is my wife’s father.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Is that right?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I knew all those Eagles that live there. Lawrence, Stoney, and those others, too, who live at Bell. Thomas Muskrat, different ones.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And also, those that lived on the mountain, those Teehee boys.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We are related.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They called him Svdi.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: And Danny.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Chutsi.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Chutsi still lives there now. Almost all of them have come down from there and live in Stilwell somewhere the rest of them. They are almost all gone, now. There are not very many of them left now. We are all related. Chutsi’s dad and my dad, Tsali, were brothers. So, when I quit there, I moved, and now I live in Siloam. I guess I will just live there now, till it is finished.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about, let’s back up for a little bit. Your grandpa and your grandma, when you were growing up, what did they do to benefit you? Like food and things like that?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Well, when we lived there, we were just children. It was hard back then. It was not easy to find anything like food or money. We just relied on the land that we had there. They called them railroad ties, we made them ourselves with an ax. I don’t know if you have ever seen anyone doing that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I have not seen anyone.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We did things like that, and posts, they called them. We cut those and sold them. When we cut the ties, we used a long, two-hand saw. We used one like that growing up. And our dad, Tsali, he used what they called a broadax. He made those ties. Made them square, like a tie.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: He would carve them.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, he made those just using that ax. Every morning, we did that. When we were little, he would take us to town when it came time for him to sell them. We had a wagon, a horse, and a mule. We would put them on there. He would take them to town. That was a long time ago. Hardly anyone has seen something like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They haven’t.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: If you were born after me you probably didn’t see it. My age is probably the end of it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How old are you?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: 75. We were just little when we started doing that. The children nowadays would not do that. What we did back then, I was just about 13 when I was already carrying those ties. When he made them, we were able to put them on our shoulders and take them to the road. And someone would pick them up for us. That is how young we were. We could do that kind of stuff. Children that age now would not do anything like that. So, we just did things like that so our dad made money. And for food, we planted a big garden about three acres in size. We planted everything, and our mom canned everything she could find. That is what we ate in the wintertime. For meat, it was deer. We killed different things for meat to eat, and we raised hogs and killed them ourselves. We butchered them. We fixed them ourselves and put them in the smokehouse for meat to eat in the winter. We did things like that and through the winter, that is how we made it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about, someone was asking and you might remember what they did. They dig potatoes about this time, ain’t it? Sometime this month, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, a little bit later. It depends on… yeah, getting close now but… In the wintertime, potatoes will last a long time. Just scatter them out on the ground or just lay them around there. And that’s how we ate them, but they lasted. They will last a long time. They lasted a long time back then. The winters are different now from how it was back then.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It is continually changing.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It was colder back then. Even the water just for ourselves.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You had your own well.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah. That long thing.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That hollow thing.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, that hollow thing we used one like that. And also a milk cow. Back then, people who had cows let them go when it turned summer. There was not a stock law yet.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: There was not hardly any fences anywhere, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: No, so they would let them go, and we would catch three of them and pen them up. But they didn’t care because they knew that was how we were getting the milk all summer. And in the winter, they would come back and get them. We would give them back. We just did things like that growing up, for food and the milk. We would set the gallon in creek water to keep cool, because we didn’t have a refrigerator. We didn’t have a cooler back then. Not even a radio. We didn’t have anything. We didn’t even have electricity yet at that time.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Even though it was like that then, do you miss it sometimes?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yes, I think about it. Even though it was hard back then, it was good for me. Sometimes I want it to be like that for a little while. I enjoyed growing up like that. Nowadays, people wouldn’t do it. They wouldn’t know what to do. We just knew how to make it back then. It is different now. People wouldn’t live like that now. They would not know how.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Nowadays, we have cell phones, and we drive good cars, and also there are places to eat.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That has made us weaker.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Back then, with no phones, they visited each other.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We just got around on foot. No matter where we went, we walked. Where our friends lived, towards the road, when we would go visit them, we walked. Or sometimes, they came to us on foot. We had roads straight through the woods. Trails to walk around on. We just did that - we didn’t have cars back then. At some point, we got some, though. I wasn’t very old when I moved. I wanted to do things myself to work.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: To help yourself.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, I wanted to help myself. I could buy what I wanted, I was thinking, if I started working somewhere. We all moved as soon as possible.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Back then, when you were just this tall [gestures], you probably knew where things were to eat? Like poke salad, things like that?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We knew everything. Back then, we knew where mushrooms grew. Some grow in the fall, and some grow in the spring. And wild onion, we ate things like that. We knew everything there was to eat. Even nowadays, I still know which mushrooms you can eat and I know those that are not good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you still eat like that nowadays? Onion, poke salad, things like that?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yes, I still do. Some have almost forgotten that now. My wife is white. She does not know how to fix things like that. If she knew how to make that bread, fried bread, I would like it. But she hardly knows how to make it. Don’t tell her that. Native women are different from white women in their cooking, but both are good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Back then, did you have… you said you did not have electricity, ain’t it, when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Not yet.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Did you use those coal oil lamps to shine light?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, coal oil - that kind of lamp, that is what we used to see at night.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And a cook stove that you put wood in?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Wood, we just used a wood stove. I don’t know if you have seen what they had a long time ago. It was like that a long time ago. It sure made good food, though.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You would surely have to split a lot of wood just this long [gestures]?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, I just made them small for that. But in the wintertime, we built a wood fire.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And also, for the heating stove.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Houses were not the way they are now. You had to have wood that we cut all winter.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And nowadays, all you have to do is just set that thing that is stuck on the wall, and it will get warm.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: For some, but I still have a wood stove.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Me too, I still use wood in the wintertime. I have one, but I use wood. I really like that better. I just grew up like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about when you were little? Back then, did your grandmother or someone know medicine, if you had an earache or a toothache?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yes, we knew everything ourselves. We didn’t go to the doctor, just the medicine we knew, if there was something wrong with us. We would just go get it. There are different things in the woods, if you know what they are.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you remember a little bit of it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, I still do, but I don’t use it anymore. I know what we also used. There was a woman who lived close by there. She was like a doctor to us. She was smart using things like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: She was a doctor back then, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: When one of the children was sick, we took them there and she would make them better. That is what we did as far as medicine - just what we knew. We didn’t go to the doctor back then. We grew up just like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And in the summertime, you would be walking around in the water somewhere, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: There was a creek there on the property where we grew up. There was a good creek, and we would swim there in the summertime. We cleaned up there. When we got dirty, we just went to the water. We didn’t have water in the house, either, at that time. That is way back in time. That is the way they lived, but nobody lives like that anymore. That is the way we grew up, all of us. There were hardly any roads, just dirt roads. But it was good. Mostly, there were just trail roads they used a long time ago.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How often did you go to town?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Not very often. Only our dad went when they took railroad ties. Then they would get food with what little money they made. We didn’t go very often. It wasn’t until I was 11 or 12 years old that I went to town the first time.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Stilwell.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What was Stilwell like back then, at first?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It was different a long time ago from what it is nowadays. They have all new buildings now. Back then, they had old buildings, like what you see on Gunsmoke. The town was like that back then. The buildings that are there now were not built yet. They tore the old ones down and built new ones. There was a café there. If we ever had money, you could just pay a quarter for a hamburger and a Coke to go with it. You could just pay a quarter and eat good. We started picking strawberries, too, and beans, green beans. There was a man named Atsiladosgi, he had a truck with sideboards on the back. He would go by early and we would ride in there and go pick strawberries.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Jim Bird was his name, Atsiladosgi. I remember him.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, Jim Bird. He had a truck. He was the only one who had a truck. He would go by early and we would ride in there. He would bring us back in the evenings. We would pay him a quarter or 50 cents for taking us, and the rest we thought we were making good money.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Where did you all go pick strawberries?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Just everywhere they had planted towards Stilwell.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They used to plant towards Rocky Mountain, I guess because of the hills.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: All the people used to do that back then. They had some planted on the edge of Stilwell. His name was Bethel Eubanks. He would call us, too. And we would go pick beans and do the same thing. That one you said, Jim Bird took us towards Arkansas and brought us back.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You all would have money when you all came back.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We would do that to make money when we started but further back, it was not that good. It was harder then. Everything got easier later.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You know, I am over 50 years old. I am not that old, but I am not a young man. Back then, I remember, in Stilwell there were more good stores.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, there were more stores. There was one named Wind Field. It was big and Isaac in the back, and in the alley there was a bar.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: There were several, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: There were things like that back then.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you remember?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I remember a little bit. They used to sell ice at that bar, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, at that bar. A block of ice.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is what they used to say. That is where they would go get them.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Rabbit Bunch was his name that worked there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is his grandfather.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Is that right? Odie Worley was the name of the one who owned that bar. If you wanted ice, you could get a block of ice there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They talked about how they used to do that.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: That was the only place you could get it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, I remember I saw all that going on. There was a gas station beside it. You had to crank that gas up to get it, that old-time gas. That was still there when I was growing up. There were things like that back then.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Back then, when people went in somewhere, they could get credit with just their word, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, it wasn’t…

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: As long as they wanted.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: If they knew you well, and you paid good, they would help you, and you could pay it back in a month. That’s the way it was. When it started to be a bank, it was hard to get money. You had to have good credit. Things like that changed. Things started to change. Like I was saying, Vernell Isaac had a store, and Wind Field, they knew my parents. They would give them credit. They knew they would pay when they got money.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Just by their word.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And also, that Washam.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, Washam.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You remember that.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, that, and Vernell Isaac, and the mercantile.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Mercantile, yeah.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I knew all of them. They are not alive nowadays. I was little, that is why I can remember that. None of the adults who were living back then are alive. I just remember them. That is just what we did growing up. They used to buy ties there, and that is where we sold ties. But they stopped buying them. My dad would carve them and make them long - about 16ft long. They built houses with them. His name was Lloyd Sam. He lived near Salem. He lived in a house where Tsali had carved the ties. You would not see anyone now, and you will never see another person doing that. They used to make them with an ax. It would be interesting if you knew someone who could do it back then. But I was just a little boy. I knew how to do that, but that ran out. No one does that anymore. I still have an ax that my dad used for carving a long time ago.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Does it still have the handle?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It doesn’t have the handle. It just broke. You can buy one like that if you look around.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Your dad said he has one, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He said they used to do that, too.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The handle has a strange bend in it, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, it kind of curves like this [gestures] so you can work it. Well, it was interesting back then.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It was good, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It was good. Me and my brother hunted for squirrels for our food. We would leave in the morning and hunt all day with dogs. Even if we did not have a gun, we would still kill them. We could throw rocks around really good back then. Growing up with just a rock, we could knock them squirrels off if they were on a tree somewhere. Even if we did not have a gun, we would bring home some squirrels. We were smart hunters. There was nothing we couldn’t do back then. I couldn’t do that nowadays. My hands ain’t worth nothing, but back then, we really could. We used to play baseball. They had teams everywhere - Greasy, Bell, Maryetta. They would meet everywhere, the Cherokee. We would just use bats they made themselves, that they whittled. We did not have good bats back then. Just homemade.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They say some could hit really hard.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: The one you said, Rabbit Bunch and all his brothers played baseball back then, at Greasy. What was his name that lived there on top of the hill? They had a big ball field, and that is where the natives met. Most of them were native boys. Them Bunch boys, all them boys, you probably know all of them. They all played, and Cherry Tree also had a team. Like them Woffords that lived there. All them people played good back then. They could play really good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That is what they…

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Those boys could really play good back then. They could hit hard. Rabbit Bunch would hit it over everything when he hit it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And also, I heard when your dad hit that ball, it would go out of sight, he would hit that hard.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That Rabbit Bunch.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Not your dad, Rainwater?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it. I remember him, too. And that place that was by Marble City.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Henderson.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We used to go everywhere playing baseball back then. Nowadays, they don’t do that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They don’t, not hardly.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It has all gone away.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Really, really. What about when you finished at Bell in the eighth grade? You went to Stilwell? Did you finish there?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, Stilwell.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: So, when you got out of the 12th grade, what did you do?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I started working. I was in a hurry to make money back then. That was enough. It was enough to finish 12th grade. You were going to do good back then. Not nowadays. Nowadays, it is different. That is not enough. Now you can go further if you want to make it. But back then, we just stopped there. That was like college for us back then. We would just start working. Then you get married, I guess, later on. That is where you went from there on. I just worked all my life. I just worked a lot of years. I probably worked 60 years before I quit.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Have you been to the army?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: No, they didn’t call me back then.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about when you finished 12th grade, where did you work?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I started going everywhere, looking for a place to work. It was not easy to find. Then I went towards Texas. Someone said, “We can find a job there.” We headed that way, and we were working there for a while. Then we would come back.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What were you all doing there?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Turkeys. We vaccinated turkeys, different things like that. You could only find things like that. There was not a lot of work back then. And also, chickens. Then I came back and started a crew of chicken catchers. I worked at Ft. Smith for three years doing that, and Springdale at Georges, doing that for 10 years. Just doing things like that. Then I found a good job in Siloam. That is why I moved there. I worked there for 30 years.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You were saying chickens. Me too. I was about 25 years old when I started. Back then, it was easy if you were young, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, it wasn’t hard. They think it is hard, nowadays. Back then, we didn’t think it was hard. It was good work, and you could make good money.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You could just go for a little while, ain’t it, and make good money.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, I just did things like that. I worked with chickens for about 15 years. Then I moved to Siloam and worked there for 30 years. When I retired from there, I was not old enough. I started working too early. I was only about 13 when I started working. When I finished there after 30 years, I worked at what they call Lowe’s. I worked there for 10 years.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: There in Siloam.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They call it medicine there in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: What is it?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: For Siloam they say medicine. That’s it, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Is that what they call it?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Medicine Siloam.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I didn’t know they called it that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That is what they call it.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I must be the only Cherokee who lives there because there are not any Cherokee there.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Where in Siloam did you work for 30 years?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: There at Franklin Electric.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I worked there for that long.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I remember when it closed down, ain’t it, about…

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It was then that I quit.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I wasn’t old enough yet. But what did you say, that's Lowe’s?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Lowe’s. The town of Siloam they call it medicine.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Oh, medicine.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: So, you worked at Lowe’s.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I worked there for 10 more years. 10, 30, and 15. I worked for almost 60 years altogether.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you go back to where you grew up sometimes?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I still go back. We still have the land where we grew up, but nobody lives there.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: There at Fog Hollow, you said.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: The natives gave us that land there. We don’t live there now, but it is still there. I watch out for it when I go there sometimes, to see if things are still OK.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: There is not hardly anyone living who is in their 70s, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The other day I went to visit Henili. Do you know Henili?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Henili, yes, I go visit him when I get time. He is getting old. He is about 84 years old.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: He is about that age. He said he doesn’t hardly drive anymore, I think.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: He is the only one living you could call an elder. And the one they called Calvin…

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I knew him.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: He also lived near there.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Calvin passed away, too.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We all grew up around there. There were a lot of Soaps and Eagles where I grew up. I enjoyed the way we grew up.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It teaches you something when you grow up like that. When you become an adult, you use what you learned.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We grew up just doing things like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You seem to appreciate it more when something good happens to you.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yes, it’s good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When you find something a little good.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I think about how we grew up. I think it’s good. It’s easy to eat nowadays. It’s not a hard life. It is easier sometimes.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Back then, people got up and hoed their gardens. They went to find food, or go fetch water, or go hunting. Nowadays, nobody hardly has a garden, or has chickens nowadays.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: That, too, we had lots of chickens. We killed one, like on Sundays, or if we wanted something to eat. We raised things like that - chickens and hogs. Sometimes, we would kill them in the winter when we were hungry. We would kill squirrels, and fish in the creek. That is what we did for meat. The rest of it we just planted.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The food that was cooked by the elders was really good.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It was good. I just appreciate how I grew up. I enjoyed it. As I remember things, we all just grew up there.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Someone was saying - I was listening to a preacher one time. He said, “It is good to eat the food that has been cooked with love.” And it is also good if they go get something that has been cooked quickly, but a long time ago.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: They used to cook all the time.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s it.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Our mom used to spend the day cooking, in the morning and at noon. She made bread all the time. Natives liked bread back then. I don’t know if it is still like that today. They made bread themselves.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And also…

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: They call them biscuits. They were good at making them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They made blueberry and blackberry pies, things like that.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We would pick things like that. Something sweet to eat.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Sometimes, I think about - I could be mistaken, but I don’t think there is as much as there was, nowadays.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: There might be, but you have to go look for it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Even like crawdads. There are not as many in the water, it seems like.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: We ate things like that, too, crawdads and fish. Crawdads are good. I would like to eat some right now.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But crawdads are going away, too.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I don’t see them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t either.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Doesn’t seem like there are that many anymore.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You can buy them at the store. But I don’t know… you can buy a big bag of them.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Is that right?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But I don’t know if they are good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The blueberry seems like it is harder to find. When it was in season, last year or two years ago, it was green when I found it. I thought, “Boy, if I come back in two days, it will be ripe,” I thought. When I came back, there was nothing there.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: The things in the woods, we ate things like that, too. There weren’t that many living out there back then. And nowadays, everyone who is in the woods will get there first, if you don’t hurry up.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They will beat you to it.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, we used to pick blackberry to eat and make sweets. And blueberry, just different things like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: There used to be wild plums, ain’t it? They would be on the side of the road somewhere.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I think they still exist, but they are harder to find. They used to make juice from those. They called them possum grapes. What do they call them in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What is that in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Uninasugi, that’s it.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Natives used to like those. They were good for making juice to drink.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Somewhere around fall, when it frosts, those are…

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Toward winter, then they are good. They ripen toward the end, and different things. Everything takes turns, so you can have food all summer. You just have to know when it comes up.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The ones that lived a long time ago had knowledge about things like that. They knew just when things would ripen, like you are saying, and they also had knowledge of the changes.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I know everything about that, about when things are going to grow, all of that. When it is just unitlogi, I know when they are in season, different things like that. We knew back then. I don’t know if anybody does, nowadays.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They probably don’t watch for it very much.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: That’s what I mean. Unless they are about my age. Then they will know.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They have been through it, y’all have been through it.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I remember that. Some who were born later know some, too. There are some that don’t know they know things. These natives that live out this way towards Salem, I know they know things like that. And also at Greasy, there are still a lot of natives who live out that way.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The oldest one that is still living is Soldier Vann.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Is he still alive?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: He still is. Did you know him?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, I knew him. I know all of them elders that are still living today. I can remember them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Cherokee speaking is getting less now, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It is really getting less. Some children can still speak out that way where I grew up, but not a lot. A few of them speak, but there are not very many. It really is running out.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Now that you have retired from working, what do you do nowadays?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I still fish all the time. I go to the water.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Which way do you go?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I go everywhere. I have a boat, a Tenkiller Grand. They call it Beaver. I go everywhere. I still do that a lot.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s good.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: That is what I used to do, growing up. I worked, but on the weekends I did that. I used to enter fish tournaments all the time.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I did that for a long time. Probably over 40 years, I was fishing and things like that. That is why I went to all the lakes.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You are living a good life then.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I been everywhere, as far as Missouri, Table Rock, Bull Shoals, all of them lakes. In Texas, I went everywhere. That is what I do. When this is over, I will show you some.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: So, you caught some big bass?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: That’s what I fished for growing up, and nowadays I still do that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Sometimes there must be some pretty good money for the prize, if you come in first?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: If you come in first, you could do pretty good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Which dam do you like to fish the most?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It was Tenkiller, but I like Grand Lake nowadays. I mostly go there, and sometimes I go here at Tenkiller. Everywhere - Beaver and where they call Eucha. I don’t go as far now. I slowed down.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do you go by yourself?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do you go fishing by yourself?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: No, someone is with me all the time. My grandson, he is yea tall [gestures], he has started going with me. We go all the time. When I get old, I am going to give him that boat I have, I think.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: He will keep going. What about that? How many children do you have?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I just have two children. I am raising my grandchildren right now, three of them. Their parents didn’t do good. I took them in, and I am raising them just like they were my own children. They are living at my house now. It’s been a while - they were just little when I took them in. They are almost grown now.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They are doing good now. There is a lot of that happening. That’s the way it is.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I am enjoying it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: When they are not there, I miss them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I guess that’s just the way it was meant to be sometimes, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: There is nothing wrong if you can treat them right. If you raise them right, it’s good. If it’s not to you, where are they going to go? Somebody has to do something.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s true, that’s true.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I just do things like that. When I get the time, I go toward the water, and if it’s not that, I just watch them. I have a lot to do at my house, but that is what I do for me, if I want to get away. I would go more than that if I could, but I have too much to do around the house. And those children, I just take them all the time, too. We are all together.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That is good that you all are living good together. You wouldn’t want anything different. Do you have several rods and reels to use for different fish?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I have a lot. I really have fished a lot, kindly way up there, I have been way up there as a fisherman. I have been everywhere.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When we were growing up, you would just have one rod and reel. It would be strange if you had two lures, ain’t it? We would be fighting over one lure.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, it was like that then, just one to fish with and just something little, and that was it. And nowadays, there is a lot of stuff. That is what I do now since I quit working. I still go three times a week.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That is a lot.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Somebody calls me all the time and asks me to fish, wanting to go fishing. I don’t run out of people. All the time, somebody wants to go and they know that is what I do. We go everywhere.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You know, if you are doing something, like fishing or hunting, if you have something to do, that keeps you going, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it. I still get around good, even though I am at that age. I have not been hindered yet. I feel as good as I felt 30 years ago.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That is joyful.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Nothing has gone down, but that is the reason why I don’t just sit somewhere. I am doing something all the time. That is what you need to do.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Very true, very true.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I have a good life. I am happy.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You seem like it. You even look good, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: That’s it, I could never forget Cherokee.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Is that right?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I try to teach those children that I have. They want to learn Cherokee. They want to learn more when we come out this way. When we get back, they will say, “Grandpa, teach us.” So that is what we are doing right now.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s good.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I can read Cherokee pretty good. I will have a rough time sometime, but I can read.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How did you learn to read? Just making an effort on your own?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Yes, on my own. My parents, too. My mother used to always read Cherokee. She would read to us in Cherokee all the time when it was nighttime, and when we were growing up, they taught them Cherokee at church. Just with that you can learn easy, if you pay attention. I knew how, and I have forgotten a little bit now, but I am fixing it. I will get to where I can read good again..I’m watching, If you give me something good, I will figure it out. I can read it and know what it’s saying.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Here nowadays, do you still talk to someone in all Cherokee?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: No, not as much. That’s what I was telling you. I am the only one who speaks Cherokee where I live. It’s not until I come this way. That is why I go visit the ones that I know who live toward Salem. We speak in all Cherokee when I go there, and then when I go home, back to English. If you don’t watch out, you will start speaking English. The reason is I have gotten used to doing that. At home, I have to speak English. They will not understand if I speak Cherokee. That is why I want Cherokee. That is why I come this way. I want to find someone who speaks Cherokee, so we can speak in Cherokee. That is why I go visit them where I grew up. Like you said, Henili, I go visit him sometimes, and we sit outside and talk Cherokee. We just do things like that. I visit people. What is his name? Sometimes when I am here, I will see someone we were talking to in Cherokee, there at the hospital the other day. I forgot their name.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: If you are here sometimes, you can just come on in.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: That is what they were telling me when I was here last week. Thursday, the second Thursday.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Are the Cherokee speakers having a meeting this Thursday?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They are.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They eat and also…

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: That is what they were telling me, to come here. “You might know some people who are here.” People speak in Cherokee. I don’t know what time it starts, but I am going to be here.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I think they start at noon, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: They said about 12, and they stay till 4, and they feed the people, they said.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The other day, Jerry Wayne was here.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: Jerry Wayne was here? We are related. We were neighbors. We grew up together. We used to ride around together with his brother they called Brim Sanders. And we used to ride around with Tom. Tom became a preacher, too, and Martin, he was a preacher, too. Yeah, we grew up there together. We lived close to each other. I know all of them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: We’d just like a little bit more. This is the last thing. What do you think is going to happen to this Cherokee we are speaking? Do you think it will keep going, or what do you think?

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: It will keep going, but it will mostly decrease, maybe. I don’t really know, but they are starting to teach people and children. I think they finally figured out they need to do that for the children who are growing up. They have to teach them, or else it’s going to be gone if we don’t do that, and if the people think like that. There will still be some here, but it is all up to us.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: True, true. You got anything?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: billy-teehee
segments.translation: I think it’s going to be alright, but we have to do something. The time has come for us Cherokee speakers. We have to do something, or else it will be gone. Let’s be thinking like that. “Don’t let it run out on us,” I am thinking.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Thank you!
